sections.title: Contribution of Psychology to Health & Social Care

blocks.x: The word 'psychology' comes from the Greek roots psyche (soul, spirit, or mind) and logos/logia (word, or study of). Psychology is formally defined as the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes.

blocks.name: Common misconceptions
blocks.def: Psychologists can read minds; psychology is just common sense; all psychologists are therapists; psychology is the same as psychiatry. All of these are false — psychology is a broad scientific discipline with many non-clinical specializations.

items: Early explanations for mental disorders drew on spirituality/divinity, philosophical models (Plato's tripartite psyche: rational, spirited, appetitive), and medical/biological models (5th-century Hippocratic medicine).
Wilhelm Wundt (1879) opened the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany — focused on sensory physiology and conscious experience. His method was introspection.
Edward Titchener (1892, US) founded Structuralism — studying the structure of the mind.
William James founded American psychology and Functionalism (functions of the mind), publishing The Principles of Psychology (1890).
Galton pioneered human intelligence testing, drawing on Darwin's theory of natural selection.
From 1900–1920, focus shifted from 'the mind' to 'behaviour'. John B. Watson founded Behaviorism, focusing on observable, measurable behaviour instead of mental processes.
Free will vs. determinism — is behaviour a result of independent decisions, or of observable, measurable causes?

The mind–brain problem — how do experiences relate to the brain? Dualism holds the mind is separate from but controls the brain; Monism holds conscious experience is inseparable from the physical brain.
Nature–nurture issue — is behaviour a result of heredity or environmental factors?

sections.title: Contribution of Psychology to Health & Social Care

items: Helps appreciate how people's understandings and needs vary, enabling individualized care.
Improves understanding of <term d="The exchange of information between people.">communication</term>, strengthening therapeutic relationships and interprofessional work.
Identifies factors affecting <term d="The effort made to manage stressful demands.">coping</term> with illness, pain, loss, and daily demands — reducing risk of stress-related illness.
Reveals what motivates health-related behaviours (smoking, diet, exercise).
Supports evidence-based interventions to improve wellbeing and help people change lifestyles.
Biopsychologist — biological factors (drugs, nervous system activity) explaining behaviour.
Clinical Psychologist — emotional/interpersonal difficulties, mental problems.
Cognitive Psychologist — memory, thinking.
Community Psychologist — social structures.
Counseling Psychologist — helping people make important decisions.
Developmental Psychologist — changes in behaviour over age.
Educational Psychologist — improvement of learning in school.
Environmental Psychologist — effects of noise, heat, crowding on behaviour.
Industrial/Organizational Psychologist — people at work.
School Psychologist — problems affecting school children.
Social Psychologist — group behaviour, social influences.
Health Psychologist — interaction between physical and psychological health.

blocks.x: Note: A Psychiatrist is a medical doctor who has specialized in diagnosing and treating mental health disorders (unlike psychologists, who are not medical doctors).

items: Palmistry — false claim that hand lines reveal personality and predict the future.
Phrenology — false claim that skull shape reveals personality traits.
Graphology — false claim that handwriting reveals personality traits.
Astrology — claims star/planet positions at birth determine personality and behaviour.

blocks.x: Parapsychology phenomena: Telepathy (mind-to-mind communication without sensory channels), Clairvoyance (knowledge of hidden objects/events), Precognition (knowledge of unpredictable future events), Psychokinesis (mind over matter), and Reincarnation (rebirth of consciousness after death).

items: Describe — naming and classifying behaviour.
Understand/Explain — identifying causes of behaviour.
Predict — forecasting behaviour accurately.
Control — altering conditions that affect behaviour.

blocks.x: Relevance: understanding oneself and patients, recognizing abnormal behaviour, providing quality care, helping patients adjust, and enriching daily life.

items: Behaviorism (Pavlov, Watson, Skinner) — focuses on observable behaviour; how organisms learn from environmental responses.
Humanism (Maslow, Rogers, May, 1960s) — each person is unique with potential for full development (self-directed growth).
Psychoanalytic (Freud) — unconscious mind; unconscious motives/conflicts determine behaviour (id, ego, superego); method: free association.
Cognitive (Piaget, Chomsky, Festinger, 1950s) — how we process, store, retrieve, and use information.
Biological — physical/chemical body changes influencing behaviour.
Sociocultural — newest approach; influence of cultural/ethnic similarities and differences on behaviour.

blocks.x: A systematic approach to obtaining knowledge, based on careful evidence collection, accurate measurement, precise definition, controlled observation, and repeatable results.

items: 1. Making observations
2. Defining a problem — stating exact procedures to represent a concept
3. Proposing a <term d="A testable prediction about the relationship between variables.">hypothesis</term> — a tentative, testable explanation
4. Gathering evidence / testing the hypothesis
5. Analyzing the data
6. Publishing results — through journals, peer review
7. Theory building — summarizing observations, guiding further research; must allow replicability

blocks.x: Research can be experimental (establishes causality) or non-experimental (shows association, not necessarily causality).

blocks.name: Experimental method
blocks.def: A controlled study where an investigator manipulates one or more independent variables to observe the effect on a dependent variableThe variable measured to see whether it changed.. Establishes cause-effect relationships.

items: Single-blind study — either the observer or participants are unaware of who received which treatment.
Double-blind study — both the observer and participants are unaware.
Experimental group — receives the treatment (independent variable). Control group — serves as comparison. Placebo group — believes they're receiving treatment, but aren't.
Placebo effect — improvement due to the mere expectation of receiving treatment.

blocks.x: Advantages of experiments: establishing cause-effect, evaluating social programs. Disadvantages: sometimes not feasible, results may not generalize, sometimes unethical to manipulate variables.
Non-experimental methods include descriptive methods (observation, case studies, surveys) and correlational studies.

items: Naturalistic observation — behaviour observed in its natural setting, researcher does not intervene.
Participant observation — the observer becomes part of the group being observed.
Observer effect — changes in behaviour caused by awareness of being watched. Observer bias — observers see/record only what they expect.
Case study — in-depth study of an individual over time; cannot be generalized to the population.
Survey research — questionnaires/interviews; subject to wording effects (subtle wording changes affect responses).
Population — the entire group being studied. Sample — the subset that participates. Random sampling — every individual has equal chance of being selected.

blocks.name: Correlational studies
blocks.def: Examine the relationship between variables using a correlation coefficient (ranging from +1.00 to −1.00). A positive correlation means both variables move in the same direction; a negative correlation means they move in opposite directions. The absolute value shows strength (a coefficient of −0.50 is stronger than +0.25). Causality cannot be inferred due to possible confounding variables.

items: <term d="Agreement to take part given with full understanding of what is involved.">Informed consent</term>
Assent (for children, mentally unstable individuals, vulnerable groups)
Anonymity
<term d="The duty to keep a person's information private.">Confidentiality</term>
Voluntary participation
Weighing benefits and risks
Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval

mnemonics.h: SLC — three cues for abnormal behaviour
lines: Statistical infrequency, personal distress, and maladaptive/impaired functioning — the three go-to criteria for spotting abnormal behaviour.

mnemonics.h: HOMER — <term d="Any consequence that makes the behaviour before it more likely to happen again.">reinforcement</term> vs <term d="Any consequence that makes the behaviour before it less likely to happen again.">punishment</term>
lines: Reinforcement always increases a behaviour; punishment always decreases it — regardless of whether something is added (positive) or removed (negative).

mnemonics.h: ABC of <term d="The view that psychology should study only observable behaviour, not private mental states.">behaviourism</term>
lines: Antecedent, Behaviour, Consequence — the basic chain behaviourists analyse to explain why a behaviour keeps happening.

mnemonics.h: DEPC — the four goals of psychology
lines: Describe, Explain/understand, Predict, Control — the four things every psychological study is ultimately trying to do.

id (Pleasure), ego (reality — 'I'), superego (morality — think '<term d="The moral principles governing how research and practice should be conducted.">Ethics</term>') — the three parts constantly negotiating behaviour.
Variable-ratio reinforcement schedules (like gambling) are the hardest to extinguish — Very Resistant to stopping.

items.d: Psychologists start by noticing and recording a pattern of behaviour worth explaining — the raw starting point of any investigation.
The observation is turned into a precise, testable question, with exact operational definitions for the concepts involved.
A tentative, testable explanation is proposed — an educated guess about why the behaviour occurs, framed so it can be proven wrong.
The hypothesis is tested — through experiments, surveys, case studies, or observation — collecting the data needed to evaluate it.
The collected evidence is examined statistically to see whether it supports or contradicts the hypothesis.
Well-supported findings are woven into a broader theory — a set of principles that explains the observations and guides future research, always open to revision.
